Prometheus Bound. Aeschylus' stark tragedy of defiance and suffering. A Titan is chained to a rock in the Caucasus as punishment for stealing fire from the gods and giving it to humanity. It's not a play of plot or action—it's a play of principle, of one figure refusing to break under unimaginable torture.

Every day, an eagle devours Prometheus's liver. Every night, it regenerates so the torment can begin again. Infinite suffering with no reprieve. And yet he will not submit to Zeus.

His crime was teaching humans to advance. Fire was not merely literal—it represented technology, knowledge, the ability to shape their own world. Zeus forbade it because he wanted humanity dependent and obedient. Prometheus stole it anyway.

But Prometheus holds another secret. He knows something Zeus desperately wants to know: the identity of a woman whose son will one day overthrow the god-king. Various figures visit him during the play—Oceanus, offering pragmatic surrender; Io, a woman transformed into a heifer by Zeus's jealousy, trapped in her own torment; the Furies themselves. Each tries to convince him to reveal the secret and gain mercy. Each fails.

Prometheus remains defiant. He declares that his suffering is righteous and Zeus's rule tyrannical. He will not trade his integrity for relief, even though that relief is the only thing that could end his agony.

The play's ending is ambiguous. Prometheus is driven into the earth by a cataclysm, but his defiance remains unbroken. He does not yield. Somewhere in the mythology, Heracles will eventually free him, though that conclusion is lost to us.

What remains is an archetype: the hero who chooses principle over survival, who refuses to bow to unjust authority no matter the cost. Prometheus Bound is perhaps the most fundamental expression of rebellion in Western literature.
